analysis.title: "We Just Have To Survive 2026 First": Goldman's Garrett Sees Seven Signs Of "Healing" As Semis Snap A 355-Day Streak
key_insights: The Nasdaq 100 fell about 7% in October, its second-worst month since the AI cycle began in early 2023, and is in its third correction of 2026. The S&P 500 fell 0.6% on the week to 7,580. NDX fell 140bps Thursday and 350bps Friday after three green sessions had added about 150bps to the S&P and 300bps to the NDX.

Semis closed down 7%-8% on Friday (depending on the Goldman desk), their third-largest day of underperformance in more than 15 years. The SOX closed below its 200-day moving average after 355 consecutive sessions above it, the third-longest streak in 10 years, and is retesting the July low. SOX forward P/E is about 16x, an AI-cycle low.

Garrett says SPX 12-month implied correlation (at-the-money forward) is about 20%, one of the lowest levels in history, and 2027 is priced as one of the least correlated 12-month periods in Goldman's dataset. The options market prices an index that sits still while single stocks move violently.

Garrett lists seven contra indicators suggesting spot weakness may be 'healing': (1) index vol catching up to single stock and credit vol, (2) net exposure rising on risk-off flow with hedge fund nets at levels that historically accompany 20%+ drawdowns, (3) stocks no longer 'crashing up', (4) index valuations catching down to earnings, (5) pockets of equities at extremes ('safe is expensive'), (6) credit specialists suggesting AI financing needs could surprise to the downside, (7) retail dip-buying turning more cautious.

Earnings drove the AI unwind: Kioxia guided Q4 bit shipments flat as data center SSDs slipped into 1Q27, Microsoft capex came in under budget on third-party capacity delays, Intel guided PC revenue down about 20% q/q with the inventory correction running into 1H27, and AMKR and Vanchip gave soft smartphone read-outs. T+1 moves were NOW -25%, INTC -30%, RDDT -30%, FFIV -20%. Callahan attributes these to crowded positioning, a truncated calendar and secular debates.

Garrett says downside volatility is now more extreme than upside volatility for large caps. Intel's average selloff has risen above its average rally (6.5% in June), and the semis ETF and QQQ average down day is again bigger than the average up day. Skew has repriced for this in the short run.

NDX 1m vol rose almost 2 vols in one session on Friday. The S&P broke its medium-term CTA threshold intraday and clients bought downside on the index and in semis. VVIX hit 124 intraday, the highest since the US-Iran war started. 0-day straddles stayed consistently priced and midterm excess variance remains nonexistent.

Wednesday's S&P straddle, covering Apple earnings and the midterms, costs 150bps, less than Friday's 180bps single-session drop. US equity options traded almost 100 million contracts on Friday, the fourth-highest volume session on record. There are 42 sessions left in 2026, with year-end straddles at S&P ±5.1%, Nasdaq 100 ±7.8% and Russell 2000 ±6.3%.

Hedge funds net bought US equities for the first time in four weeks (+1.1 SDs), but Macro Products were 73% of it and it was mostly short covering. US-listed ETF shorts fell 4.8%, the largest covering in more than six months. Tech buying was about 40% of what hedge funds sold in the prior three weeks, and Mag 7 was net sold in four of the last five sessions, though Mag 7 length remains near year-to-date highs.

US fundamental L/S net leverage is 47% (7th percentile of the past year), gross is 216% (66th percentile). Garrett's regression of PB nets against S&P drawdowns shows these net levels have been associated with drawdowns above 20%, while the S&P is about 3% from its high.

Goldman's shares desk sold a net $4.2B of tech delta Friday, with ETFs at about 31% of tape (highest since June). The S&P closed 35 handles above its medium-term CTA threshold and the NDX closed below both its short- and medium-term triggers. Garrett expects a 'red sweep across equity systematics' when models update Monday.

On Thursday 406 S&P constituents closed green and the index still fell, with 80% of stocks higher. The S&P ex-AI basket is at highs while Goldman's AI winners basket rolls over, and ex-AI stocks were headed for their best month since 2022. TLT shows about a -0.7 two-week correlation to AI winners.

The S&P is up 10.7% on the year but its forward P/E is about 19x, the lowest of 2026. The dividend yield factor is in its 90th percentile and valuation in its 80th (10-year), while momentum (30th) and growth (40th) are cheap. The S&P Low Volatility index trades at a growth-like forward multiple.

Callahan's names to watch for the week: AAPL (36x forward P/E, all-time high, 17x premium to the S&P, reports Monday), UBER (sold off after 8 of its last 10 prints, about 10x EV/EBITDA), NET (consensus Q3 growth easing to about 32% from 36%), MCHP, TTWO. His working list of non-AI names: AAPL, SNPS, ADI/TXN/NXPI, SPOT, V/MA, EBAY, LYV.

Garrett expects the midterms to be 'a non event at the index levels' but good for basket trades. The suggested pair is long renewables and grid, and buy protection on hyperscalers and datacenter equipment, because who pays for datacenter power is an underappreciated election-sensitive theme. Kalshi prices 65% odds of a Democratic sweep per the shares desk.

The ZeroHedge write-up concludes that positioning argues for healing but flows say the unwind is not done: desks still selling tech, Mag 7 length near highs, CTAs about to flip red. It leans toward more downside until systematic selling clears.

tension_points.what_invalidates: A red sweep across equity systematics when models update Monday, or the S&P losing its medium-term CTA threshold (35 handles below), would confirm the unwind continues.
